practical_skills: Reading a lease section by section

sections.skill: Read key lease terms and apply security deposit rules

questions.prompt: A lease says: "Rent $1,100 due on the 1st. Late fee $50 if not received by the 5th." Jen pays on the 7th. What does she owe for that month?
questions.intro: A lease lists the rent, due date, grace period, late fees, length of the lease, who pays which utilities, rules (pets, guests, noise), maintenance duties, renewal terms, and what happens if you leave early. Read every section before signing.
questions.topic: Reading a lease and security deposits
sources: New Jersey Department of Community Affairs (Truth in Renting): In New Jersey, a security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent, and the landlord must return it with interest, less itemized charges, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. (https://www.nj.gov/dca/codes/publications/pdf_lti/t_i_r.pdf)

questions.prompt: A security deposit is…

choices.text: money held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear
a fee the landlord keeps no matter what condition the unit is in
a payment for the landlord's insurance

questions.correct_answer: money held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear
questions.intro: A security deposit protects the landlord against unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. It is generally returned, minus allowed deductions, after the lease ends. State laws limit amounts and set return deadlines.
questions.feedback: Deposits are held and returned minus allowed deductions.

sources: New Jersey Department of Community Affairs (Truth in Renting): In New Jersey, a security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent, and the landlord must return it with interest, less itemized charges, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. questions.prompt: In New Jersey, a security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent. Rent is $1,200. What is the largest deposit allowed?
questions.intro: New Jersey law caps security deposits at 1.5 months' rent. Other states have different limits.

questions.prompt: Jen's lease ends. Her $1,500 deposit has $200 deducted for a broken door and $0 for small nail holes. In New Jersey, about how much should she get back, and by when?

choices.text: $1,300 whenever the landlord chooses to pay

questions.intro: Normal wear and tear (small nail holes, faded paint) is generally not deducted. Damage beyond that can be. New Jersey requires the landlord to return the deposit with interest, less itemized charges, within 30 days after the lease ends.
questions.feedback: $1,500 − $200 = $1,300, plus any interest, with an itemized list, within 30 days in New Jersey.

questions.prompt: A "grace period" for rent means…

choices.text: days after the due date before a late fee applies

questions.intro: A grace period is a short time after a due date during which payment is still accepted without a late fee.
questions.feedback: Grace periods delay late fees for a few days.

questions.prompt: Why should Jen document the unit's condition with dated photos at move-in?

choices.text: To post them online for future renters
To ask the landlord to lower the rent right away
Because photos replace the need for a lease
To show which damage existed before she moved in

questions.correct_answer: To show which damage existed before she moved in
questions.intro: A move-in checklist and dated photos protect your deposit by recording existing damage.
questions.feedback: Records prove pre-existing damage so it is not charged to you.

questions.intro: Leaving early can mean paying rent until a new tenant is found or paying an early-termination fee, depending on the lease and state law.

questions.prompt: Two roommates sign one lease for $1,600 rent. One stops paying. What can the landlord usually do?

choices.text: Collect only half from each roommate, no matter what
Collect from the paying roommate only her half
Hold either roommate responsible for the full rent

questions.correct_answer: Hold either roommate responsible for the full rent
questions.intro: When roommates sign the same lease, each is often responsible for the full rent ("joint and several" liability).
questions.feedback: On a joint lease, each tenant can be held responsible for all of the rent.
